Before we start

What your business needs in place.

Transformation fails for organisational reasons, almost never technical ones. These are the four that decide it.

A sponsor who can overrule

Every transformation reaches a point where a department must give something up. Without someone senior enough to settle that, the programme stalls at exactly that step — and no technology fixes it.

Access to the people doing the work

A few hours each from the people who actually run the process. Programmes designed from the top get built correctly and used reluctantly.

Honest numbers, or permission to measure them

How long a step takes, how often it is redone, what an error costs. If nobody knows, measuring is the first stage — but pretending the numbers exist is how a roadmap becomes fiction.

An appetite for the answer being 'do less'

Sometimes the finding is that a process should be deleted rather than digitised, or that a tool you already pay for does the job. If that answer is unwelcome, the assessment will not be worth its price.

How it runs

Six steps, and you see each one.

  1. 01

    Measure

    Map the processes as they run and count what they cost. No recommendation before there is a number.

  2. 02

    Roadmap

    Stages ordered by payback, each with a cost, an outcome and a way to tell whether it worked.

  3. 03

    First stage

    Build the highest-payback change and put it in use. Proof before commitment.

  4. 04

    Adoption

    Training, documentation and the follow-up week where people actually change how they work.

  5. 05

    Next stages

    Repeat in order. Each stage funded by the one before it wherever possible.

  6. 06

    Review

    Quarterly, against the numbers we started from. Including the stages that should be dropped.

Right fit, wrong fit

Saves a call that would end in no.

A good fit

  • The business runs on spreadsheets, WhatsApp and memory
  • You have bought software before and it went unused
  • You want proof from a first stage before a large commitment
  • You need someone vendor-neutral, with no licence commission
  • Someone senior is genuinely willing to own the changes

Not a fit

  • You need a deck for a board and not the work behind it
  • The decision to buy a specific platform is already made
  • Nobody senior can overrule a department
  • You want it finished in a quarter

After launch

After the last stage.

A programme is not finished when the last stage ships — that is when drift starts. Quarterly review against the original numbers, or the fractional CTO arrangement if you want the decisions owned continuously.

Questions

The ones people actually ask.

How is this different from a consultancy?

A consultancy sells you the roadmap and then sells you the delivery, usually with a licence attached. Here the assessment is fixed-price and portable, I take no vendor commission, and every stage ends in working software rather than a status report.

What if the assessment says we should do nothing?

Then it says that, and it has saved you far more than it cost. It has happened: the finding was that two people and a better spreadsheet template beat the platform under consideration.

How long does a programme take?

The assessment is weeks. The first stage is usually a month or two. The full programme depends entirely on how many stages you choose to run, and you decide that one stage at a time rather than at the start.

Do we have to use AI?

No. AI is one option among several and it is the wrong one more often than the market admits. It goes in the roadmap only where it beats the alternative on cost or quality, and the assessment says which steps those are.

Our last transformation failed. Why would this be different?

Usually because it started with a platform decision rather than a measurement, or because nobody senior could make a department give something up. I ask about both before quoting, and if the second one is missing I will say the programme is not ready.
